newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Study sees zinc, lead heading for tough times.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Study sees zinc, lead heading for tough times.

text.p: The zinc and lead markets are in for a number of tough trading years, with prices for both metals seen falling in 1997, an industry study said on Monday.
Zinc and lead industries faced major restructuring over the next 10 years as producers react cautiously to changes in demand fundamentals, the report, by AME Mineral Economics Proprietary Ltd, said.

The accelerating impact globally of environmental legislation aimed at reducing risks from hazardous chemicals and abating air contamination threatens to encourage end users of the metals to find replacement materials, AME said.
Zinc prices should fall marginally to around US$0.47 a pound in 1997, before remaining flat for the next 10 years, AME figures showed.
Buoyancy in prices for lead, resulting from a surprise rise in battery replacement demand, would be short-lived, AME said.
That pressure would come to an end soon, leaving lead to trade at an average 34 cents a pound in 1997, five percent below the 1996 forecast of 36.3 cents.
By 2005, lead price would have fallen to an average 33.6 cents a pound.
Meanwhile, efforts by zinc and lead miners to reduce costs have had mixed result.
In the last four years, zinc prodcution costs have fallen 25 percent, although lead costs rose 4.6 percent, AME said.
AME sees prices deteriorationg despite predicting zinc and lead markets would remain in balance throughout this period.
By 1998, inventories of zinc would only represent around eight weeks worth of consumption and lead would be down to six weeks.
Zinc demand was dependent on the construction market, particularly roads and motor vehicles, AME said.
Demand for zinc from the important construction markets would be flat among developed countries, although it should rise in the developing regions of Asia and Latin America, AME said.
By 2000, zinc demand in developing countries should reach three million tonnes a year, advancing to 3.5 million in 2005, it said.
Environmental regulations were set to dictate constraints on both supply and demand, AME said.
Regulatory action would affect the use of lead in batteries and also restrict international trade in both recycled lead and zinc, which might be defined as hazardous chemiclas, AME said.
By 2000, 1.5 million tonnes of new zinc mine capcity would come on stream, AME said.
Smelting capacity over the same period would grow by 1.3 million tonne, it said.
